prompt: In `staging.api.codeschool.ing`, which part was registered from a registrar?
hint: Read the name from the right.

choices.text: `codeschool.ing`
choices.why: The pair: the label and the top-level domain it sits under.

choices.text: `staging.api.codeschool.ing`, since the whole name is what was bought
choices.why: Subdomains are created afterwards, freely, by whoever holds the domain.

choices.text: `ing`, which is the part a registry sells to whoever asks for it
choices.why: A registry runs the TLD and does not sell the TLD itself.

choices.text: `api.codeschool.ing`, because the leftmost label is added by the hosting provider
choices.why: Nothing about a subdomain requires a hosting provider at all.

prompt: What does a root server know about `codeschool.ing`?
hint: Ask what each level is responsible for.

choices.text: That it exists, and that it was registered under `ing` at some point
choices.why: The root has no record that any particular domain exists.

choices.text: Which servers run `ing`, and no more than that
choices.why: Every level knows one thing: who to ask next.

choices.text: Its address, which it keeps so that popular names are answered in one step
choices.why: Nothing about popularity is held at the root; addresses live at the bottom.

choices.text: Which servers answer for it, so that a resolver is sent straight there
choices.why: That is what the `ing` servers hold; the root is a level above.

prompt: Fill the blank: browsers ship a published list of where one owner’s territory ends, so that a page cannot set a cookie for something like `.com` — the public ___ list.
hint: It is the part of the name at the end.

prompt: A site answers on both `example.com` and `www.example.com`, with neither redirecting to the other. What does that cost?
hint: They are two different names, and software knows it.

choices.text: Twice the hosting, because each name is served by a machine of its own
choices.why: Both names can point at one machine, and usually do.

choices.text: A slower first load, since the browser resolves both names before choosing one
choices.why: A browser resolves the name it was given and no other.

choices.text: Two sets of cookies, two sessions, and two entries in a search result
choices.why: Three costs, and the choice of which name is canonical barely matters.

choices.text: No cost; browsers treat a bare domain and its `www` name as the same site
choices.why: Nothing treats them as the same, which is the whole difficulty.

prompt: Which of these are true about the characters in a domain name? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three rules, each of which saves an argument.

choices.text: Case is ignored entirely
choices.why: `CodeSchool.ing` and `codeschool.ing` are one name.

choices.text: A label may not begin or end with a hyphen
choices.why: Letters, digits and hyphens, and not at the edges.

choices.text: Names in other alphabets work, carried by a translation into a restricted one
choices.why: Which is where the odd `xn--` names in logs come from.

choices.text: A name may hold at most three labels
choices.why: There is a length limit and no limit on the count.

choices.text: Spaces are permitted as long as the whole name is quoted
choices.why: There is no quoting, and no spaces.

prompt: What did you get when you bought a domain?
hint: The word owner does not appear anywhere in the arrangement.

choices.text: Ownership of the name, recorded at the registry and transferable like property
choices.why: It is recorded and transferable, and it is not ownership and does not last.

choices.text: A block of addresses that the name resolves to for as long as you hold it
choices.why: No addresses are included; where the name points is a separate arrangement.

choices.text: A licence from the registrar, which the registry has no part in
choices.why: The registry holds the record, which is what matters on the bad days.

choices.text: The exclusive right to have that name delegated to your servers, for a period
choices.why: Everything odd about domains follows from the last three words.

prompt: Match each party to what it does.
hint: One of the three is you.

pairs.right: Runs one top-level domain and holds the real list
The shop, accredited to write into that list
The person or company the name is recorded to

right_distractors: The organisation that assigns addresses to networks
The provider that answers queries for the domain

prompt: A company misses a renewal and the domain is taken by somebody else. Which loss is the serious one?
hint: Think about what else runs on a domain.

choices.text: The mail
choices.why: Whoever holds the name receives every password reset ever sent to it.

choices.text: The site, which stops answering the moment the name changes hands
choices.why: Visible, immediate, and the least of the three.

choices.text: The certificates, which are issued against the name and stop being valid for it
choices.why: A consequence worth knowing, and not the one that opens accounts.

choices.text: Search engines drop the site, which takes months to recover once the name is back
choices.why: Real and recoverable, and it assumes the name comes back.

prompt: Fill the blank: a registration that lapses spends a ___ period, during which it can still be recovered at a penalty, before it is released.
hint: It is the word for buying something back.

prompt: Why should the contact address on a domain not be an address on that same domain?
hint: Ask what fails at exactly the moment you need to be told.

choices.text: Because registries reject a contact address inside the domain being registered
choices.why: Registries accept it; it is a bad idea rather than a refused one.

choices.text: Because the address stops receiving mail exactly when the warnings are sent
choices.why: Losing the domain would also lose the only channel that would tell you.

choices.text: Because registrar notices are filtered as spam when they arrive at their own domain
choices.why: A plausible annoyance, and not the failure this avoids.

choices.text: Because a domain's own mail is delivered without leaving the provider, so it is not logged
choices.why: Delivery paths vary and none of that is what makes this a rule.

prompt: Which machine in a lookup does the walking from root to answer?
hint: Your own machine asks once and waits.

choices.text: The authoritative server, which asks the levels above it to confirm its own answer
choices.why: It answers from its own records and confirms with nobody.

choices.text: Your machine, which follows each referral in turn until it reaches an answer
choices.why: It asks one server and waits; it follows nothing.

choices.text: The recursive resolver
choices.why: It chases the answer and hands you a single result.

choices.text: The root server, which goes and fetches the answer on the resolver's behalf
choices.why: The root answers *ask them* from a list it holds and fetches nothing.

prompt: Put the steps of a cold lookup in order.
hint: Each of the first three answers *not me, them*.
items: The resolver asks a root server, which names the servers for the TLD
The resolver asks a TLD server, which names the servers for the domain
The resolver asks an authoritative server, which answers with the address
trap: It is tempting to put the authoritative server first, because it is the one that knows. Nothing knows where it is until the two referrals above it have been followed, which is why the walk exists at all.

prompt: Fill the blank: the plain-text question travels over ___ on port 53, which is why anybody on the path can read every name you look up.
hint: Three letters, and lesson six explains why it fits.

prompt: Why does a popular name usually cost one question rather than four?
hint: Something between you and the root already knows.

choices.text: Browsers ship a list of common names and their addresses, refreshed on update
choices.why: No such list ships, and it would go stale immediately.

choices.text: The TLD servers answer with the address directly when the domain is well known
choices.why: A TLD server answers with a referral whatever the domain is.

choices.text: Root servers keep addresses for the most requested names, answering them directly
choices.why: The root holds no addresses for domains, popular or otherwise.

choices.text: The resolver already holds the answer, or at least the referrals
choices.why: A resolver serving a hundred thousand people learned this seconds ago.

prompt: What is the honest account of moving your lookups to DNS over HTTPS?
hint: Two true things at once.

choices.text: It hides the questions from the network and concentrates them in fewer hands
choices.why: Both halves are true, which is why it is contested rather than simply better.

choices.text: It makes lookups faster, because HTTPS connections are reused between questions
choices.why: Sometimes faster and sometimes slower, and speed is not the argument.

choices.text: It is required by browsers now, so the trade-off is no longer anybody's to make
choices.why: Browsers ship it and some enable it; it remains a setting.

choices.text: It removes the record of what you look up, since no log survives the encryption
choices.why: The provider answering still sees every question; nothing is removed.

prompt: Match each record type to the question it answers.
hint: One of them is the delegation itself.

pairs.right: What other name should I ask about?
Where does mail for this domain go?

right_distractors: What certificate authorities may issue for this name?
What address does this name map back from?

prompt: Why can the bare domain not carry a `CNAME`?
hint: Two rules meeting.

choices.text: Because a bare domain is resolved through the TLD servers, and those hold no aliases of any kind
choices.why: The TLD servers hold referrals, and that is not what forbids this.

choices.text: Because an alias shares its name with nothing, and `NS` records are there
choices.why: Which is why so much hosting documentation quietly insists on `www`.

choices.text: Because an alias adds a second lookup, and the bare domain is resolved before the others
choices.why: Nothing resolves the bare domain first; there is no such ordering.

choices.text: Because registries forbid it, to stop a domain being pointed outside its own zone
choices.why: It is a rule of the record types rather than anything a registry decides.

prompt: An `MX` record is written with an address instead of a name. What happens?
hint: The type takes one kind of value.

choices.text: The record is accepted and the priority is ignored, so messages go to one place
choices.why: The priority is unrelated, and the record's value is the problem.

choices.text: Mail is delivered to that address, more slowly, because a reverse lookup is needed first
choices.why: Nothing performs that lookup, and delivery does not happen at all.

choices.text: It fails
choices.why: An `MX` names a server, and putting an address there is not a valid record.

choices.text: It works until the address changes, at which point the record has to be updated by hand
choices.why: It does not work at any point, so there is nothing that later stops working.

prompt: Fill the blank: the record type used to publish a string proving you control a domain, and to carry SPF, DKIM and DMARC, is `___`.
hint: Three letters, and it was originally just a place to put a note.

prompt: Which of these are true of an `MX` record? Choose all that apply.
hint: One number, one name, and two rules.

choices.text: A lower priority number is preferred
choices.why: 10 is tried before 20, which is how a backup is expressed.

choices.text: It points at a name rather than at an address
choices.why: Putting an address there is not a valid record.

choices.text: The name it points at should not itself be an alias
choices.why: A rule people break precisely because an alias looks like the tidy way.

choices.text: It is consulted when a browser loads the site
choices.why: The address records answer that; this one is consulted by mail servers.

choices.text: A domain may have at most one
choices.why: Several is the normal arrangement, which is what the priorities are for.

prompt: A record with a TTL of 300 is changed. What is the longest anybody waits?
hint: Nothing is pushed anywhere.

choices.text: Until each resolver is restarted, since a cached answer is held in memory
choices.why: A cached answer expires on its own clock without any restart.

choices.text: It varies by distance, with nearby resolvers updating well before distant ones
choices.why: Distance plays no part; the timers started at different moments.

choices.text: Forty-eight hours, which is how long the change takes to reach each resolver
choices.why: Nothing travels between resolvers, so nothing takes time to reach them.

choices.text: Five minutes
choices.why: One TTL, counted from the change, and the number was yours to choose.

prompt: Why does a change appear for some people and not others?
hint: Ask when each resolver started its clock.

choices.text: Because each resolver’s copy expires at a different moment
choices.why: Whenever the first person on that network happened to ask.

choices.text: Because some resolvers refuse a change until the old record has been removed
choices.why: A resolver is not told about removals and has nothing to refuse.

choices.text: Because the change is written to the TLD servers first and the root servers later
choices.why: Neither of those holds your records, so neither is written to.

choices.text: Because resolvers are updated in waves, beginning with the largest providers
choices.why: There are no waves and no updating; each resolver asks again on its own.

prompt: Fill the blank: lowering the TTL has to be done at least one *old* TTL before the move, because that change is itself held for the ___ period.
hint: The one that was in force before.

prompt: You look up a name, get nothing, then create the record. Why might it take longer to appear than usual?
hint: Something was cached that was not a record.

choices.text: The record inherits the domain's default TTL, which is longer than the one you set
choices.why: A new record carries the TTL you gave it.

choices.text: The absence was cached, with a length from the domain's own defaults
choices.why: So the useful habit is to create it first and check afterwards.

choices.text: The resolver refuses a name that changed from missing to present within its cache window
choices.why: No such refusal exists; it simply has not asked again.

choices.text: Creating a record takes effect at the authoritative servers before the TLD servers
choices.why: The TLD servers hold no records of yours, so there is nothing to wait for there.

prompt: Where does the forty-eight-hour folklore actually come from?
hint: One TTL in this system is not yours.

choices.text: From registrars, which batch their writes to the registry overnight
choices.why: Writes go through promptly; the delay is in the caching above.

choices.text: From resolvers, which are required to hold an answer for at least a day
choices.why: There is no such minimum; a resolver honours the TTL it was given.

choices.text: From the TTL the registry puts on your `NS` records at the TLD servers
choices.why: Accurate for exactly one change: moving your domain to another DNS provider.

choices.text: From the root servers, which are refreshed from the registries twice a day
choices.why: The root holds nothing about your domain and refreshes nothing on your behalf.

prompt: Match each answer to what it means.
hint: One of them looks like an answer and contains nothing.

pairs.right: The name exists and has no record of that type
Something broke, or an answer was disbelieved

right_distractors: The name exists and you may not ask about it
The record was found and has expired

prompt: A resolver returns the old address and the authoritative server returns the new one. What should you do?
hint: The difference between the two answers is the diagnosis.

choices.text: Clear the cache at the registrar, which is what holds the answer resolvers are serving
choices.why: A registrar holds no cache that resolvers read from.

choices.text: Point the `NS` records at a different provider to force the resolvers to ask again
choices.why: That is a far larger change and would be held by an even longer timer.

choices.text: Change the record again, since a record that resolvers disagree about was written wrong
choices.why: The record is right; rewriting it would reset nothing and change nothing.

choices.text: Wait
choices.why: The change is published and you are inside a TTL.

prompt: A site is broken for people on one resolver and fine for people on another, with no geographic pattern. What does that suggest?
hint: Some resolvers check something that others do not.

choices.text: Signatures that a validating resolver refuses and a non-validating one ignores
choices.why: Nearly a signature of the fault, and the reason the second-opinion question answers it.

choices.text: A TTL that expired on one resolver and not the other, so one has the new record
choices.why: That produces a wrong answer rather than a failure, and it resolves itself.

choices.text: A firewall blocking port 53 for some networks, which is why some lookups fail
choices.why: That would break every name for those people, rather than one site.

choices.text: A record with several addresses, one of which points at a machine that is down
choices.why: That would break for people at random rather than by resolver.

prompt: Fill the blank: a name written in a record file without a trailing ___ has the domain appended to it, which is how `mail.provider.net` quietly becomes something that does not exist.
hint: One character.

prompt: A change appears to succeed in the control panel and reaches nobody. What is worth checking first?
hint: There can be two control panels.

choices.text: Whether the record was saved, since some panels require a second confirmation step
choices.why: Worth a glance, and it would not explain a change that appears to succeed.

choices.text: Which servers are authoritative for the domain
choices.why: The old provider's panel still works and is read by nobody.

choices.text: Whether the TTL was set low enough for the change to be picked up
choices.why: A TTL delays a change and does not prevent one.

choices.text: Whether the domain is inside its renewal window, which freezes edits until it is paid
choices.why: No such freeze exists as part of renewal.

prompt: You are moving a site to a new host tomorrow. What do you do today?
hint: One step, and it costs nothing.

choices.text: Raise the TTL, so that resolvers hold the new answer once they have it
choices.why: Backwards: a high TTL is what makes the old answer linger.

choices.text: Point the `NS` records at the new host so the delegation is ready in advance
choices.why: That moves every record at once, which is the slow change rather than the fast one.

choices.text: Lower the TTL on the records you are about to change
choices.why: It waits out the old TTL, which is why it has to be today.

choices.text: Create the records at the new provider and leave both sets in place for a day
choices.why: Two providers answering is a different problem rather than a smooth move.

prompt: Which of these are needed to put a small company on one domain? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four destinations, four kinds of line.

choices.text: An `A` record for the site
choices.why: A name to an address.

choices.text: An `MX` record for the mail
choices.why: A priority and a server name, not an address.

choices.text: A `CNAME` for the documentation service that gave you a name
choices.why: An alias: go and ask about that one instead.

choices.text: A separate registration for each subdomain
choices.why: Subdomains are free and immediate under a domain you hold.

choices.text: A `PTR` record so the site answers on the bare domain
choices.why: A reverse mapping, unrelated to serving anything.

prompt: Fill the blank: the `NS` records are the delegation itself, which is why pointing them at a new provider moves ___ your records at once — including the ones nobody copied across.
hint: One word, and it is why mail stops.

prompt: Which command tells you what you published rather than what the world believes?
hint: Skip every cache between you and the truth.

choices.text: A trace from the root, which shows each referral in turn
choices.why: Genuinely useful, and it tells you the path rather than settling this question.

choices.text: A lookup with the cache disabled in the browser's developer tools
choices.why: That setting is about the browser's own resources, not about names.

choices.text: A lookup through a public resolver you do not normally use
choices.why: A useful second opinion, and still a cache.

choices.text: A lookup addressed to the authoritative server itself
choices.why: It separates *my change is wrong* from *my change is not live yet*.

prompt: A record has a TTL of 600 seconds. What is the longest, in minutes, that somebody can keep serving the old value after you change it?
hint: One TTL, converted.

prompt: Somebody says the site is down and the address works when typed directly. Where is the fault?
hint: Ask which step failed.

choices.text: In the name resolution
choices.why: The machine is answering; what failed was turning a name into it.

choices.text: In the certificate, which is issued for the name rather than for the address
choices.why: True of certificates, and it would show as a warning rather than a failure to load.

choices.text: In the hosting, which is reachable by address and not configured for the name
choices.why: Possible, and it would produce a response rather than nothing at all.

choices.text: In the browser's own cache, which is holding a failure from an earlier attempt
choices.why: Worth clearing, and it would not explain the same fault for other people.

prompt: Why is a domain with empty mail-authentication records a problem even if you send no mail?
hint: Ask what somebody else can do with the name.

choices.text: Receiving mail stops working, because recipients refuse a domain without them
choices.why: Receiving is decided by the `MX` records and is unaffected.

choices.text: Anybody at all is able to send mail claiming to be from you
choices.why: The most consequential empty setting in the lesson.

choices.text: The registrar suspends the domain after a period without any records of that kind
choices.why: No registrar requires them, and none suspends for their absence.

choices.text: Certificates stop being issued, since some authorities verify by mail to the domain
choices.why: Mail verification is one option among several and does not depend on these.

prompt: Put these in the order they happen when you open a page on a name nobody has asked for lately.
hint: Two of them are finished before the connection exists.
items: The name is resolved to an address
A connection is opened to that address
trap: It is tempting to put the connection first, because that is where the lesson-six story began. The name has to become an address before there is anything to connect to, and on a cold cache that is several round trips of its own.

prompt: A name resolves correctly for everybody except the person investigating it. What should they look at?
hint: Something on their own machine is consulted first.

choices.text: The TTL, which may have expired for others and not for them
choices.why: An expiry gives them a newer answer rather than a different one indefinitely.

choices.text: Their browser's cookies for the domain, which can pin it to an earlier address
choices.why: Cookies hold no addresses and have no part in resolution.

choices.text: The `hosts` file on their machine
choices.why: Consulted before DNS, and genuinely useful right up until it is forgotten.

choices.text: Their resolver, which may be filtering the name for the whole network
choices.why: That would affect their colleagues on the same network too.

prompt: Which record type would you use to point `docs.example.com` at a service that gave you a name rather than an address?
hint: Go and ask about that one instead.

choices.text: An `NS` record, delegating that subdomain to the service's own servers
choices.why: A heavier arrangement that hands them the whole subdomain.

choices.text: An `MX` record, since the target is named rather than addressed
choices.why: Named, yes, and that type is consulted for mail alone.

choices.text: An `A` record, with the address you resolve from their name once
choices.why: It works until they change it, and they will not tell you.

choices.text: A `CNAME`
choices.why: An alias, and it is fine here because it is a subdomain.

prompt: Why is a long TTL on `MX` records usually the right choice?
hint: Weigh a change you rarely make against an outage you might.

choices.text: Because the cushion during a DNS outage is worth more than a fast change
choices.why: You change these once a decade and want them cached when something breaks.

choices.text: Because a short TTL on an `MX` causes messages to be delivered out of order
choices.why: Ordering of mail has nothing to do with how long a record is cached.

choices.text: Because the priority numbers stop working when the record is refreshed often
choices.why: Priorities are part of the record and are unaffected by its lifetime.

choices.text: Because mail servers refuse records with short lifetimes as a sign of abuse
choices.why: No such refusal exists in mail delivery.

prompt: What is the single most useful thing about holding a domain, for somebody building things?
hint: It is about what comes after the purchase.

choices.text: The registration protects the name against similar ones being registered nearby
choices.why: It protects that exact name and nothing resembling it.

choices.text: Every name under it is yours to create, free and immediately
choices.why: A new environment or a new service is a line in a file you control.

choices.text: The domain carries a reputation that new subdomains inherit for mail delivery
choices.why: Partly true for mail and not the general point being made.

choices.text: Certificates are issued for the domain and cover the names beneath it
choices.why: Only when a wildcard was requested, and it is a separate purchase.
